narrative:
The model determined that you have a 72% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were admitted. Your first-year ranking in the third decile also worked against you, though with less force, again falling short of the sixth-decile average seen in successful applicants.

Your LSAT score of 30.5 was the only factor that pulled the prediction in a more positive direction. While helpful, it was not large enough to offset the two academic-ranking signals.

In short, the model concluded that your law-school grades placed you at higher risk of struggling with the bar exam, and this risk outweighed your other strengths.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your class rank in the remaining years, consider a structured bar-preparation course early, and retake the LSAT if you can raise your score meaningfully. Once those numbers move closer to the averages of admitted students, reapply. Many candidates improve their profiles and are admitted on a second attempt.
